big: Rohan holds a ₹100 bond that pays 8%. Then new bonds start paying 9%. Nobody wants his 8% bond at ₹100 any more. To sell it, he must cut the price. This one idea explains most of the bond market.

lines: I thought a bond was safe. Why can its price fall?
Safe from default is one thing. Safe from price changes is another. When market rates rise, old bonds with lower coupons lose value. They move like a seesaw.

alt: Bars showing the price of a two year and a ten year bond after rates rise
caps: Both bonds pay 8% and are priced at ₹100.
Rates in the market rise to 9%.
The 10-year bond falls further, to about ₹93.6. Longer bonds are more sensitive.

rows: The yearly return if you buy at today's price and hold to maturity
Rising rates push the prices of existing bonds down
How sensitive a bond's price is to rates. Higher means more
Interest received may have to be reinvested at lower rates
note: Prices here are made up from a standard formula, to show the idea. They are not forecasts.

q: Market rates rise. What usually happens to the price of Meena's existing bond that pays a lower coupon?
why: A rise would make sense only if market rates had fallen.
New bonds pay more, so old ones must be cheaper to attract a buyer.
Prices of existing bonds do move when rates change.
Doubling has no link to a small change in rates.

q: Which bond is likely to fall more when rates rise by 1%?
opts: A bond that matures next week
why: A shorter bond has a lower duration, so it reacts less.
A bond close to maturity is hardly affected by a change in rates.
They do not fall equally, since duration differs.
A longer bond has a higher duration, so its price reacts more.

q: Rohan buys a bond below its face value and holds it to maturity. What does the yield to maturity tell him?
opts: The yearly return at his price
Only the coupon rate printed on the bond
The profit if the bond is sold next week
why: Yield to maturity includes the coupon and the gain from the price he paid.
The coupon alone ignores the price paid, which changes the return.
A quick sale depends on the price then, so the yield does not tell him this.
Tax is a separate matter from the yield on the bond.

q: Meena's bond pays a coupon, and rates have fallen. What is the reinvestment risk?
opts: The bond losing all of its face value
The issuer changing its name soon
The coupon being paid twice a year
why: Face value is repaid at maturity, and reinvestment risk is not about that.
A change of name has no link to reinvestment of interest.
When rates fall, the interest she receives may earn less when reinvested.
A coupon is paid once on its date, so this is not the risk.

pts: When rates rise, existing bond prices fall, like a seesaw.
Longer bonds, with higher duration, move more.
Yield to maturity counts the price you paid.
